item.title: First three derelict vessels cleared for removal from Suva Harbour
item.description: Work to remove the first three derelict vessels from Suva Harbour is set to begin after the Derelict Vessel Removal Project Governance Committee approved the next phase of the long-awaited clean-up initiative. The vessels are the first of 17 identified derelict vessels earmarked for removal under the Captain Johnathan Smith Fund, marking a significant milestone in efforts to restore Fiji’s busiest
item.content:encoded:
Work to remove the first three derelict vessels from Suva Harbour is set to begin after the Derelict Vessel Removal Project Governance Committee approved the next phase of the long-awaited clean-up initiative.

The vessels are the first of 17 identified derelict vessels earmarked for removal under the Captain Johnathan Smith Fund, marking a significant milestone in efforts to restore Fiji’s busiest harbour.

The Governance Committee met last week to finalise preparations and coordinate the next stage of the project, which brings together the Government, maritime agencies and environmental partners.

Permanent Secretary in the Office of the Prime Minister, Dr Lesikimacuata Korovavala, said extensive planning had been necessary before work could commence.

“This has been a long time coming, but we had to ensure the right foundation was laid for such an undertaking to stand on.”

Dr Korovavala said the project also honours the legacy of Captain Johnathan Smith.

“The Captain Johnathan Smith Fund is carrying on the legacy of an esteemed member of our society, in the hope that the future will be a bit brighter for those who watch the sunlight reflecting on the Suva Harbour.”

The meeting follows the completion of an operational agreement outlining how the clean-up will be coordinated between the Government of Fiji, the Joint Maritime Environment Committee, Fiji Ports Corporation Limited, the Maritime Safety Authority of Fiji, the Waitt Institute and Blue Prosperity Fiji.

Fiji Ports Corporation is leading the operational phase, including overseeing contractors responsible for cleaning and scuttling the vessels in accordance with Fiji’s legal requirements.

Authorities say vessels will only be scuttled after meeting strict environmental and safety standards certified jointly by the Department of Environment and the Maritime Safety Authority of Fiji, and only at approved locations.

Permanent Secretary for Environment and Climate Change, Dr Sivendra Michael, said removing the abandoned vessels demonstrates Fiji’s commitment to protecting its marine environment.

“For far too long, these abandoned vessels have posed risks to traditional custodians, marine ecosystems, navigation and public safety, and their removal is helping to restore the ecological integrity.”

The Government will continue to oversee the project through the Joint Maritime Environment Committee, while the Waitt Foundation has contributed US$1 million to establish the Captain Johnathan Smith Fund. Blue Prosperity Fiji is supporting coordination of the initiative as part of Fiji’s broader marine spatial planning and ocean management programme.

item.title: Proposed Bill gives Commission wider search powers
item.description: The proposed Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026 would grant the Commission expanded powers to enter and search premises, seize evidence and access computers during investigations, as nationwide public consultations continue. Under the draft legislation, Commission officers would be permitted to enter and search premises with the consent of the occupier, under a court-issued warrant, or
item.content:encoded:
The proposed Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026 would grant the Commission expanded powers to enter and search premises, seize evidence and access computers during investigations, as nationwide public consultations continue.

Under the draft legislation, Commission officers would be permitted to enter and search premises with the consent of the occupier, under a court-issued warrant, or without a warrant in urgent circumstances where there are reasonable grounds to believe evidence could be lost or destroyed.

The Bill would also allow Commission officers to search individuals in public places without a warrant if they reasonably believe it is urgently necessary to prevent the destruction or loss of documents or other evidence relating to an alleged breach of the law.

The proposed powers are designed to strengthen the Commission’s ability to investigate anti-competitive conduct and consumer protection offences.

During a search, Commission officers would be authorised to use reasonable force to enter premises where legally permitted, examine documents or other items, take photographs or video recordings, and undertake any action reasonably necessary to carry out the investigation.

The legislation would also require occupants to provide officers with full and unrestricted access while a lawful search is being conducted.

Anyone who obstructs or interferes with a Commission search could face significant penalties.

Individuals convicted of obstruction could be fined up to $50,000, jailed for up to 10 years, or both, while companies could face fines of up to $500,000.

The Bill also recognises the growing importance of digital evidence by giving Commission officers the authority to use computers and other electronic devices found during a search.

Where officers have reasonable grounds to believe it is necessary, they would be able to operate computers to locate, examine and copy electronic documents, provided doing so would not damage the equipment or stored information.

The proposed powers would also extend to documents that can be lawfully accessed through a computer, including records stored remotely at another location.

The nationwide consultation process, that starts today gives businesses, consumers, legal practitioners and other stakeholders the opportunity to provide feedback on the proposed legislation before it is finalised.

item.title: Failure to cooperate could attract $50,000 fine or 10 years in jail under proposed bill
item.description: Individuals who fail to comply with investigation notices issued by the Competition and Consumer Commission without a reasonable excuse could face fines of up to $50,000, imprisonment for up to 10 years, or both, under the proposed Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026, which enters nationwide public consultation today. Companies that fail to comply could be fined up to $500,000 upon convi
item.content:encoded:
Individuals who fail to comply with investigation notices issued by the Competition and Consumer Commission without a reasonable excuse could face fines of up to $50,000, imprisonment for up to 10 years, or both, under the proposed Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026, which enters nationwide public consultation today.

Companies that fail to comply could be fined up to $500,000 upon conviction.

The draft legislation proposes significantly stronger enforcement powers for the Commission, including expanded investigative authority and tougher penalties for those who obstruct or refuse to cooperate with investigations.

Under the proposed Bill, the Commission would have the power to investigate any conduct it believes may constitute a breach or offence under the Act.

The Commission would also be required to investigate complaints lodged by members of the public but could decline to do so if it considers the complaint unwarranted, impractical, a poor use of resources, or if it is deemed trivial, frivolous, vexatious, lacking in substance or contains insufficient information.

The Bill also allows the Minister to refer matters directly to the Commission for investigation. If the Commission determines it does not have the resources to conduct the investigation, it must notify the Minister as soon as reasonably practicable.

The proposed legislation introduces new safeguards for people under investigation.

Before questioning anyone who may face prosecution or financial penalties, the Commission would be required to advise them that they have the right to remain silent, are not required to answer questions, and that anything they say or do may be used as evidence in future legal proceedings.

Any evidence obtained without first providing the required warning would generally not be admissible in criminal proceedings or proceedings seeking financial penalties.

The Bill also empowers the Commission to compel individuals and organisations to produce documents or other material relevant to an investigation through a written notice.

Such notices must outline the purpose of the investigation, specify when and where documents must be produced, and clearly state the penalties for failing to comply, providing false or misleading information, or destroying evidence.

Public consultations on the proposed Bill begin today, giving businesses, consumers, legal practitioners and other stakeholders the opportunity to provide feedback before the legislation is finalised.

The proposed Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026 aims to modernise Fiji’s competition and consumer protection laws while strengthening the Commission’s ability to investigate anti-competitive conduct and protect consumer interests.

item.title: Proposed Bill allows FCCC to seize computers during investigations
item.description: The proposed Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026 would empower Commission officers to secure computers and other electronic equipment for up to 72 hours during investigations where there is a risk that digital evidence could be destroyed or tampered with. The provision forms part of the draft legislation now open for nationwide public consultation.
item.content:encoded:
The proposed Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026 would empower Commission officers to secure computers and other electronic equipment for up to 72 hours during investigations where there is a risk that digital evidence could be destroyed or tampered with.

The provision forms part of the draft legislation now open for nationwide public consultation.

Under the proposed law, Commission officers would be able to secure electronic equipment found during a lawful search if they have reasonable grounds to believe the equipment contains evidence relevant to an investigation, expert assistance is required to access the information, and delaying action could result in the evidence being destroyed, altered or otherwise interfered with.

The Bill would allow officers to secure the equipment for up to 72 hours. If more time is needed, they would be required to apply to a magistrate for an extension.

Commission officers would also be authorised to take whatever steps are reasonably necessary to secure the equipment, including locking it away, placing it under guard or using other appropriate measures.

The proposed legislation requires officers to notify the occupier of the premises that the equipment will be secured, advise that it may remain secured for up to 72 hours, and inform them if an application will be made to extend that period.

Any extension beyond the initial 72 hours could only be granted if a judge, magistrate or justice of the peace is satisfied that additional time is necessary.

The Bill also outlines new procedures for obtaining search warrants.

Under the proposal, judges, magistrates or justices of the peace would have the authority to issue warrants authorising the search of premises, vehicles, vessels, aircraft or other places upon application by a Commission officer.

Search warrants would remain valid for no longer than seven days, with the expiry date required to be specified on the warrant. New warrants could be issued where necessary.

Applications for warrants would generally be made in writing and supported by sworn evidence. However, where appearing in person is impractical, applications could also be made electronically, by telephone or by other appropriate means.

The nationwide consultation process gives businesses, consumers, legal practitioners and other stakeholders the opportunity to comment on the proposed Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026 before it is finalised.

item.title: Court dismisses former FRCS officer’s employment claim
item.description: The Employment Court has dismissed a claim by former Fiji Revenue and Customs Service (FRCS) employee, ruling that the organisation did not breach the principles of equal employment opportunity or fair labour practices when it appointed another candidate to the position of Senior Customs Officer. In a judgment delivered on 23 July, Justice Vishwa Datt Sharma found that FRCS had followed its recrui
item.content:encoded:
The Employment Court has dismissed a claim by former Fiji Revenue and Customs Service (FRCS) employee, ruling that the organisation did not breach the principles of equal employment opportunity or fair labour practices when it appointed another candidate to the position of Senior Customs Officer.

In a judgment delivered on 23 July, Justice Vishwa Datt Sharma found that FRCS had followed its recruitment policy and standard operating procedures throughout the selection process.

The case centred on the worker’s claim that he was unfairly overlooked for the position after being made redundant in December 2021. He argued that FRCS had denied him a fair opportunity for employment and career advancement by appointing another candidate and later advertising the position again.

However, the court found that the successful applicant had outperformed the worker during the recruitment process.

Justice Sharma noted that “all candidates undergo recruitment process and those who meet the MQR are shortlisted for aptitude test and interview and the interview is conducted and assessed by three panel members.”

Rejecting the worker’s allegations, Justice Sharma ruled: “I do not find that the Defendant, Fiji Revenue and Customs Service, by not appointing the Plaintiff… acted in any breach of the principles of equal employment opportunity and fair labour practices.”

The court dismissed the worker’s application and ordered that each party bear its own legal costs.

The ruling also confirmed that the worker had received a redundancy package following his compulsory redundancy in December 2021, including one week’s pay for each completed year of service, a $2,000 ex gratia payment, salary up to his final day of employment and other statutory entitlements.

item.title: Harvesters query rate cut
item.description: MECHANICAL harvesting operators will need to seek clarification from the Fiji Competition and Consumer Commission (FCCC) over the recent review of harvesting rates, says Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna. Mr Tunabuna was responding to concerns from operators after FCCC revised the mechanical harvesting rate from $24.63 a tonne to $20.52 a tonne following a decline in fuel prices.
item.content:encoded:
MECHANICAL harvesting operators will need to seek clarification from the Fiji Competition and Consumer Commission (FCCC) over the recent review of harvesting rates, says Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna.

Mr Tunabuna was responding to concerns from operators after FCCC revised the mechanical harvesting rate from $24.63 a tonne to $20.52 a tonne following a decline in fuel prices.

The revised rate represents a 16.7 per cent reduction from the previous interim rate.

Some operators have raised concerns that the reduction could affect their ability to provide harvesting services.

Mr Tunabuna said FCCC was responsible for explaining the basis of the review and how the revised rates were calculated.

“I’m not sure how they formulate their formula charges. They will have to explain.”

He said adjustments to harvesting rates were part of the normal review process and were linked to changes in fuel costs.

“The fuel subsidy that was given to them will be readjusted when there is a change in fuel. That’s very normal practice.”

Mr Tunabuna said stakeholders should engage with FCCC over the revised rates, as mechanical harvesting operators remained an important part of the sugar industry.

item.title: Sugar sector row pits Chaudhry, Prof Biman
item.description: FORMER prime minister and National Farmers Union general secretary Mahendra Chaudhry has criticised Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka over discussions to privatise the Fiji Sugar Corporation, accusing him of making statements without taking action. Mr Chaudhry questioned Mr Rabuka’s understanding of the sugar sector following comments about a possible sale of the State-owned sugar miller to a private
item.content:encoded:
FORMER prime minister and National Farmers Union general secretary Mahendra Chaudhry has criticised Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka over discussions to privatise the Fiji Sugar Corporation, accusing him of making statements without taking action.

Mr Chaudhry questioned Mr Rabuka’s understanding of the sugar sector following comments about a possible sale of the State-owned sugar miller to a private entity.

He claimed that despite establishing a Special Parliamentary Committee on Sugar in July last year to address long-standing industry challenges, the Prime Minister had not convened a meeting of the body.

“He hasn’t called a single meeting of that committee since it was formed,” Mr Chaudhry said. “If he says he is trying to privatise the industry to sell it to somebody, I don’t think he understands the situation properly.”

Mr Chaudhry accused the Prime Minister of ignoring cane growers while challenges in the industry continued.

However, National Federation Party leader and Parliamentary Sugar Select Committee member Professor Biman Prasad rejected Mr Chaudhry’s criticism, saying he was responsible for the decline of sugar industry institutions.

“He is the man who was responsible for the destruction of the sugar industry institutions,” Prof Prasad said.

He defended the committee’s work, saying members, chaired by the Prime Minister, had conducted field visits across Viti Levu to meet growers, with visits to Vanua Levu planned.

He said the committee was assessing both immediate relief measures and long-term strategies for the industry.

Prof Prasad said sugarcane farmers under the current administration had received the highest cane prices in the country’s history, with further recommendations being considered to address challenges, including the impact of the fuel crisis.

Questions sent to Mr Rabuka remained unanswered when this edition went to press last night.

item.title: Tunabuna hits out at NFU’s absence
item.description: NATIONAL Farmers Union (NFU) general secretary Mahendra Chaudhry has been vocal on social media about issues affecting the sugar industry but did not attend consultations with farmers and stakeholders, says Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna. Mr Tunabuna made the comments in response to Mr Chaudhry’s recent statement calling on the Government to address concerns raised by cane farmers and challenges f
item.content:encoded:
NATIONAL Farmers Union (NFU) general secretary Mahendra Chaudhry has been vocal on social media about issues affecting the sugar industry but did not attend consultations with farmers and stakeholders, says Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna.

Mr Tunabuna made the comments in response to Mr Chaudhry’s recent statement calling on the Government to address concerns raised by cane farmers and challenges facing the sugar industry.

Mr Chaudhry had criticised the Government’s response to harvesting difficulties and said concerns over cane prices and payments needed to be addressed to improve cane supply.

However, Mr Tunabuna said he was disappointed Mr Chaudhry did not participate in discussions despite claiming to represent farmers.

“He can be very vocal on social media, but he hasn’t really been coming forward,” Mr Tunabuna said.

He said Mr Chaudhry had written to Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka and copied him on a letter outlining several demands before the crushing season.

“He clearly mentioned that they were not boycotting, but they had their demands, and they were going to harvest. Their demands were met.”

Mr Tunabuna said he had attempted to arrange a meeting with Mr Chaudhry to discuss the issues raised.

He said consultations were later held with farmers and transport service providers in various areas, involving the Prime Minister, Opposition Leader, senior Government officials and Members of Parliament.

“Although he said he was representing farmers, he was not in any of those forums.”

Mr Tunabuna said it was disappointing that concerns were being raised publicly when opportunities were available for direct discussions with stakeholders.
